title: Vertebrate Limb Adaptations
question: How can shared bone positions and model proportions help us compare a human arm, bat wing and dolphin flipper?

blocks.prompt: Required before handling the models: Can an arm, wing and flipper have corresponding bones even when they work differently? Predict which part of a bat wing might support its broad membrane.
blocks.text: The arm, wing and flipper may keep corresponding bones despite different uses. Long bat digits might support its membrane.

blocks.prompt: Required before handling the models: Why should you compare corresponding regions rather than just the longest bone? Why could drawings at different scales make raw lengths misleading?
blocks.text: Compare corresponding positions and use the same supplied humerus reference. Raw picture lengths alone could differ because of drawing scale.

Handle and grasp objects.
Correct after feedback. Five separate digit rays include a thumb that can oppose the fingers. This helps with handling objects. The drawing shows a selected open-hand pose.

Support a membrane during flight.
Correct after feedback. Long digits support a skin membrane. The thumb remains short and free. The radius is long; the ulna is reduced and partly fused with it. Shape and muscle control both matter in flight.

Steer and stay steady in water.
Correct after feedback. Digits remain inside a shared soft-tissue flipper. Some have extra phalanges. Flippers help steer and keep the body steady in water; they are not shown as the main source of forward thrust.
Identify corresponding forelimb regions despite differences in shape and use.

blocks.prompt: Compare the humerus, forearm and wrist/digit regions in all three models. What positions remain similar? Explain how the reduced bat ulna and extra dolphin phalanges modify the shared pattern without creating unrelated structures.
blocks.text: My homology explanation uses the supplied forelimb models. Corresponding upper-arm, forearm and wrist/digit positions support the shared pattern despite different forms. The bat ulna is reduced and its long digits support a membrane; the dolphin has extra phalanges within some digits and a steering flipper. My diagram spans 80, 270, 180 units give ratios 0.80, 2.70, 1.80 to the supplied 100-unit reference. These constructed values are not real-animal averages or performance measurements. Common ancestry does not make a living human the ancestor of a living bat or rank fitness.

blocks.prompt: What makes these forelimb regions homologous?
blocks.text:
Their corresponding structures were inherited from a shared ancestor, even though their uses may differ.
Correct! Homology concerns shared origin. Shapes and functions can change in descendant lineages. Living humans, bats and dolphins each have their own evolutionary history. Correct on first recorded check.

blocks.prompt: What does a ray-to-humerus ratio compare in this lab?
blocks.text:
A constructed diagram span relative to its supplied 100-unit upper-arm reference.
Correct! Dividing a span by a reference length compares proportions. These illustration values are not calibrated measurements of real animals or performance. Correct on first recorded check.

blocks.prompt: A dolphin digit contains more phalanges than a human finger. What does that mean?
blocks.text:
More small bones along that digit, not necessarily more digits.
Correct! Phalanges are bones within a digit. Extra phalanges can lengthen a digit inside a flipper. A changed form does not create an evolutionary ranking. Revised after feedback.

These are original simplified teaching drawings, not X-rays, measured specimens or species averages. The supplied humerus reference is 100 diagram units in every rescaled model. Third-digit ray spans of 80, 270 and 180 diagram units are constructed illustration values, not published measurements. Bone widths, poses, joint details and soft tissues are simplified. The selected ray is straightened, so its end-to-end span is defined for this drawing; other poses could change the span seen in a flat view. Tags annotate existing parts; they do not add or move real bones. The bat ulna is reduced; it is not drawn as a second full-sized radius. Some dolphin digits have extra phalanges, which does not mean extra fingers. These models illustrate shared ancestry and modified form but do not reconstruct a complete family tree or measure force, speed, flight efficiency, survival or fitness. A living human is not the ancestor of living bats or dolphins. No physical dissection or measurement protocol is supplied.
